summary: CODEC combines integrated-gradients-style contribution scores at hidden neurons with a sparse autoencoder that decomposes those contributions across inputs, and applies the pipeline to ResNet-50, ViT-B, and retinal CNN models. The method is well-motivated as an alternative to activation-based SAE interpretability, and the ablation/preservation experiment plus the retinal dynamic-receptive-field analysis provide non-trivial evidence that contribution modes carry causal information activations do not. However, the paper suffers from thin positioning against modern interpretability baselines (activation SAEs, circuit analysis, path patching), essentially no reported variance/statistical tests, an ImageNet perturbation story that hinges heavily on one class in the main text, and a ViT result that is admitted to underperform and buried in supplements, all of which soften the generality claims.
strengths: The core methodological move — running an SAE over integrated-gradients-style contributions rather than activations — is a clean and well-motivated twist that leverages IG's completeness property to obtain per-channel signed effects on the output.

The ablation/preservation study (Fig. 6) provides a genuinely causal check: contribution modes require fewer channels to knock out or preserve class accuracy than activation modes, which directly supports the paper's central 'causal not correlational' framing.

Applying the same framework to a retinal ganglion-cell CNN and using it to explain dynamic instantaneous receptive fields via mode combinations is a distinctive cross-domain contribution that extends the paper beyond a standard ImageNet interp study.

The layerwise phenomenology — sparsity, dimensionality, and progressive decorrelation of positive vs. negative contributions — is a novel empirical observation about how CNN computations reorganize with depth.

key_concerns.issue: Related work is under-developed and does not seriously position CODEC against the modern SAE interpretability literature (Bricken/Cunningham/Templeton-style activation SAEs), attribution/circuit-analysis methods (path patching, causal scrubbing, ACDC), or prior 'attribute-then-decompose' pipelines. The reader is left unsure what specifically is new vs. combining known ingredients.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add an explicit related-work section that names and contrasts (i) activation SAEs for feature discovery, (ii) attribution methods extended to hidden units, and (iii) circuit-style causal interpretability, stating precisely which element of CODEC is novel and which components are borrowed.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical rigor is thin: figures report point estimates (sparsity, correlations, dimensionality, ablation curves) without seeds/error bars or significance tests, and the SAE-hyperparameter robustness is described qualitatively rather than quantified with variance across seeds. Given that SAEs are known to be seed-sensitive and that the claim is 'modes are more class-aligned/more causal than activation baselines,' variance reporting is essential.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report multi-seed runs for the SAE training (both contribution and activation baselines), include confidence intervals in Figs. 3, 5, 6, and add a paired significance test for the contribution-vs-activation comparisons in the ablation/preservation experiment.

key_concerns.issue: The ImageNet perturbation narrative in the main text leans heavily on the 'black widow' example, with the class-generalized story compressed into Fig. 6D–E and a claim of taxonomic generalization deferred to supplementary. This is exactly where reviewers expect breadth: per-class distributions, worst-case classes, sensitivity to number of channels ablated, and comparison to non-mode baselines (random channels, top-activation channels, top-gradient channels).
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Move a class-distribution summary of ablation/preservation efficacy into the main text and add stronger baselines beyond activation-modes: random-channel ablation matched for count, top-activation channels, and top-|gradient| channels.

key_concerns.issue: The generality claim is weakened by the ViT results being admitted to be worse than CNN results and deferred almost entirely to the supplement. Given the ICLR audience, ViT (and ideally at least one language-model layer) is where interpretability generality is judged.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either scope generality claims tightly to CNNs + retinal CNNs, or present ViT results in the main text with a fair analysis of why perturbation is weaker (spatial-reduction strategy, token vs. channel structure), plus at least a preliminary LLM-layer demonstration matching the promise made in the limitations section.

key_concerns.issue: Writing quality is uneven — several run-on sentences, missing spaces after commas, and typos ('retinl', 'selecte channels', broken math formatting in the input-visualization derivation) impede reading and would need a careful editorial pass.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Copy-edit throughout; re-typeset the sensitivity/contribution-map equations with proper LaTeX; break long compound sentences in the introduction and methods.

key_concerns.issue: Reproducibility of the retinal experiment is weaker than the ImageNet experiment: the CNN retinal model, target choice (surprisal), and clustering procedure are described only briefly, and the number of cells/sessions/mice used is not stated in the main text.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a compact 'retinal experimental setup' subsection specifying the source dataset, number of ganglion cells, train/test split, stimulus type, and the k-means/silhouette details used to obtain the three clusters.

questions_for_authors: How do contribution modes compare quantitatively (in the Fig. 6D metric) against non-trivial baselines beyond activation SAEs — specifically top-|gradient| channels, top-activation channels, and random channels matched for count?
How stable are the identified modes across SAE seeds and across independent runs on disjoint halves of ImageNet? Do the class-correlated modes replicate?
For the retinal analysis, is the claim that modes drive dynamic IRFs supported by a held-out stimulus split, or is it descriptive of the training set? How many cells/sessions are analyzed?

What is the precise novelty relative to attribution-based hidden-unit analyses (e.g., Tanaka 2019, Maheswaranathan 2023) that already used integrated gradients on hidden units? Is CODEC's contribution specifically the SAE decomposition step, and if so, how does it compare against non-SAE decompositions (NMF, PCA with rectification, dictionary learning) on the same contribution matrices?
In Fig. 3C–D, is the progressive decorrelation of positive/negative contributions robust to the choice of contribution algorithm (ActGrad, SmoothGrad, IG) and to the number of IG integration steps?
For the ViT results in the supplement, what fraction of the CNN-style causal gains survive, and how sensitive is this to the tokens-as-space choice?
calibration_check: Claims are mostly scoped to the presented evidence, but the abstract/intro phrasing ('general-purpose framework', 'scales to any feedforward model', 'state-of-the-art models of neural activity') is stronger than the ViT and LLM evidence actually shown in the main text.

significance.justification: A causal-contribution SAE that bridges CNN interpretability and computational neuroscience is a genuinely interesting angle, but the impact hinges on whether the ablation-based causal gains reproduce beyond ResNet-50, which is not yet convincingly shown.

novelty.justification: Neither integrated-gradients-on-hidden-units nor sparse autoencoders are new; the specific composition (SAE over signed contribution vectors, then use loadings as causal handles) is a reasonable and non-obvious combination, but not a conceptual leap.

rigor.justification: The method is internally coherent and uses completeness of IG correctly, but several claims (progressive decorrelation, mode-based causal superiority) rest on point-estimate comparisons without controlling for confounds like channel count or activation magnitude.

statistical_soundness.justification: Almost no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported for the main quantitative claims; SAE robustness is described qualitatively; the ablation comparison to activation modes lacks paired variance analysis.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations are acknowledged (ViT underperformance, restricted blocks, LLM only in supplement), but the abstract and framing still claim generality and 'state-of-the-art models of neural activity' more strongly than the main-text evidence supports.

clarity.justification: The high-level story is understandable, but heavy run-on sentences, typos, malformed equations, and captions that describe several distinct claims at once make the technical presentation harder to follow than an ICLR paper should be.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows a recognizable intro/method/experiments/conclusion arc, though there is no dedicated related-work section, and the retinal and ViT sections read as appendices lifted into the main text.

reproducibility.justification: SAE architecture, thresholds, learning rate, batch size, and IG-step count are given; datasets are standard; but retinal-model setup, clustering details, and per-experiment hyperparameters are underspecified in the main text.

related_work.justification: Modern SAE interpretability, circuit analysis, and causal-intervention literatures are essentially absent; the contribution is not clearly delineated against Tanaka-2019/Maheswaranathan-2023, which already used IG on hidden units in retinal CNNs.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe informative analyses (layerwise sparsity/dimensionality, ablation curves, IRF dynamics), but they pack multiple claims per figure and mostly show point estimates rather than distributions or seed variability.

breadth_generality.justification: Three domains are touched (CNN, retinal CNN, ViT), but ViT is admitted to underperform, LLMs are deferred entirely to supplementary, and the CNN causal story is anchored on one architecture and one dataset — weaker than the 'general framework' framing requires.

overall_recommendation.justification: A borderline submission: the method is a reasonable and thought-provoking contribution with a nice cross-domain application, but missing baselines, thin statistics, weak ViT generality, and under-developed positioning against modern interpretability work keep it below the ICLR acceptance bar as submitted.
